extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of political science / public institutions
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic, descriptive treatment of how the U.S. House of Representatives works: the Speaker's role, committee appointment and function, debating conditions, party organization (or lack thereof), and legislative effectiveness. Intended as a chapter-length exposition of institutional features and evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee appointments should reflect important groups and regions
rubrics_metrics.description: Appointments to committees should compliment important groups of men or types of opinion and should give a place on good committees to their prominent representatives; nominations should avoid alarming particular interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains political constraints on committee selection: the Speaker (or appointing body) must balance party, state, and sectional interests; failure to do so creates trouble and anxiety. Hybrid committees may be appointed partly by the House and partly by the Committee of Selection; private bill committees by the Committee of Selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker must exercise power with fairness to opponents
rubrics_metrics.description: Although expected to serve his party, the Speaker must not resort to all possible means and 'must not palpably wrest the rules of the House to [the majority's] disadvantage.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific duties: give opponents a reasonable share of 'the floor' (debate) and concede proper representation on committees. He may decide doubtful points against opponents, but overtly abusing rules is disallowed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of Speaker as a politically significant event
rubrics_metrics.description: The selection of the Speaker is a political event of much significance; the whole policy of a Congress can turn on whether the man selected represents divergent tendencies in the majority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because chairmanships and committee distributions are influential, the Speaker's selection matters for the course of domestic events and party leadership within the House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speaker's authority: wide scope but variable duration
rubrics_metrics.description: The Speaker's power can be far-reaching in capable hands and may rival the President in influence in ordinary times, though shorter in duration and less patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical note: Speaker's authority has been reduced over time but remains significant and may regain former extension depending on circumstances and occupants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical debating conditions affect quality of oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: Large chamber size, seating, galleries, and acoustics make it hard for ordinary voices to be heard; only a powerful and well-trained voice can fill the hall.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: speakers often rely on written speeches or remain silent; the room's size discourages detailed oral exposition and favors declamatory set speeches. Changes to furniture (removal of desks, chairs replaced by benches) affect attention and oratorical dynamics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set speeches tend toward declamation rather than argument
rubrics_metrics.description: A set speech on an important subject tends to become a piece of elaborate and high-flown declamation rather than a practical exposition or argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: authors often send full texts to reporters and print them in the Congressional Record, distributing copies to constituents; this saves time but reduces substantive oral debate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short, time-limited debates are often more effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Five-minute debates (when imposed) in Committee of the Whole on bills reported from standing committees are often lively, pointed, and effective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast with long, purposeless speeches on large questions; time limits can produce practical, focused exchanges on taxation and appropriations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Most practical legislative work is done in standing committees
rubrics_metrics.description: Standing committees handle the practical business of legislation; much of the House's time on the floor is consumed by pointless discussions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees serve as the locus of detailed work and prepare measures for floor consideration; committee reports and internal expertise guide members who lack subject knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee chairs act as leaders pro hac vice
rubrics_metrics.description: When a matter referred to a committee comes before the House, the chairman of that committee is treated as a leader for that subject and members unfamiliar with the issue are apt to be guided by his speech or advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If committee advice is unavailable or suspect (e.g., chairman from opposite party), members look to the member in charge of the bill or trusted colleagues for direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Committee system substitutes for party organization
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of a European-style party leadership, the committee system provides organization and a way to make large assemblies work promptly and smoothly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is described as one of three methods for managing large deliberative bodies (leave few questions to the assembly; organize by parties/leaders; or divide into smaller bodies/committees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of clear government/opposition leadership
rubrics_metrics.description: The House has parties but they are 'headless' — there is neither Government nor Opposition in the European sense; there were no whips until about 1900 and no ministers sit in the House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical effect: no permanent unofficial representative responsible for marshaling votes or securing quorums; majority may be opposed to the President and there is no official daily executive representative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of leaders weakens responsibility and organisational efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Without leaders and whips, responsibility for neglect of business or mismanagement is diffuse; critics argue this contributes to hesitations, inconsistencies, and failures in Congress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterargument from American statesmen: failures may reflect divisions of public opinion and Congress's role as following, not leading, the nation; responsibility is therefore diffuse by constitutional design and political culture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties usually vote solid on major national issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Though the House lacks tight leader control, on large national issues where party sentiment has been declared, both majority and minority generally vote solid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On minor issues there is more latitude; when a serious issue arises the majority often takes a recess to caucus and then returns to vote solidly according to the caucus decision; surprises and scratch votes still occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: House tends to avoid grave and pressing questions; follows public opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The House tends to skirmish around serious questions rather than face them, reflecting a national temperament that representatives should not move faster than their constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: European observers see this as failure to lead; American reply: Congress mirrors divisions and waits for clearer public mandates before acting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of empty resolutions and performative bills
rubrics_metrics.description: Assemblies will indulge in speeches addressed to galleries and bills meant to be circulated but not seriously proceeded with; the House is particularly apt to pass superfluous or complimentary resolutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: harmless but obtrusive condolence resolutions; electioneering bills; sometimes absurd proposals to achieve impossible objects — often intended to humor a section of opinion rather than effect policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Turnover of members affects legislative efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: High turnover (historically many new members each Congress) reduces legislative efficiency; although re-election rates have increased, turnover has been a notable feature affecting experience and continuity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data example: In the Sixty-first Congress (1909-11) only 74 out of 391 had not served before; sixteen had served nine or more previous terms. Increased re-election raises continuity and capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical furniture and layout shape member attention and decorum
rubrics_metrics.description: Desks encouraged inattention by enabling members to write letters; removal of desks and replacement of chairs with benches brought members closer together and altered behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large galleries and seating arrangements also influence how far voices must carry and how members interact; small adjustments (furniture, galleries) have practical impact on debate quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of printed record and circulation of speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Members often send full written speeches to reporters and have them printed in the Congressional Record, then distribute copies to constituents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice saves time and ensures their views reach the public even if oral delivery in the chamber is ineffective; there are limits (e.g., policy changes after abuse — printing curtailed when a member printed a poem).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative criterion: House as a 'fair average sample' vs European 'governing class'
rubrics_metrics.description: Americans conceive the legislature as a fair average sample of the country and expect it to follow public opinion; Europeans expect legislatures to consist of the best men and to lead the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This represents a normative criterion for evaluating the House's role: whether it should lead or follow public opinion, and explains many institutional differences (lack of ministers, different expectations of leadership).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three institutional methods to make large assemblies work
rubrics_metrics.description: Three methods: (1) leave few questions to the assembly and reserve others to smaller bodies/executive officers; (2) organize into well-defined parties with leaders; (3) divide the assembly into smaller bodies (committees) to which questions may be referred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The U.S. House relies mainly on the third (committee) method, partly combined with the second; chapter frames committee system as the chosen mechanism for efficiency in large modern legislatures.
